prompt: `String[] titles = new String[3];` What does each element hold before anything is assigned?
hint: `Arrays.toString` printed them.

choices.text: An empty string, `""`
choices.why: An empty string is an object; a new array of a class type holds no object at all.

choices.text: `null`
choices.why: Right: `[null, null, null]`, the default for any class type.

choices.text: Nothing: reading one before assigning it is a compile error
choices.why: Array elements always have a default; it is local variables that must be assigned first.

choices.text: Whatever was in that memory before, as in C
choices.why: Java fills every new array with defaults, so there is no leftover memory to see.

prompt: `int[] years = {1899, 1881, 1943};` Which expression is the last element, whatever the array's length?
hint: Positions start at 0.

choices.text: `years[years.length]`
choices.why: That is one past the end, and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

choices.text: `years[3]`
choices.why: It is one past the end for this array, and it is not general either.

choices.text: `years[years.length - 1]`
choices.why: Right: it printed `1943`.

choices.text: `years[years.length() - 1]`
choices.why: `length` on an array is a field, without brackets; this does not compile.

prompt: `System.out.println(years)` printed `[I@25b485ba`. What is that?
hint: An array is an object without its own way to describe itself.

choices.text: The type's code name, `[I`, and a number from the array's identity
choices.why: Right: and the number differs on every run. `Arrays.toString` prints the elements.

choices.text: The memory address where the array is stored
choices.why: It is derived from the object's identity and is not an address you can use; it changes between runs too.

choices.text: A sign the array was corrupted by the earlier assignment
choices.why: Nothing is corrupted; the next line printed the elements correctly.

choices.text: The sum of the elements, written in hexadecimal
choices.why: 1899 + 1880 + 1943 is not 25b485ba in any base; the number has nothing to do with the contents.

prompt: Reading index 3 of a three-element array throws `Array___Exception`.
hint: Index ... out of bounds.

prompt: A program creates `int[] shelves = new int[5];` and later needs a sixth shelf. What can it do?
hint: The length is fixed when the array is created.

choices.text: `shelves[5] = 0;`, which grows the array by one
choices.why: Index 5 is past the end of a five-element array: it throws.

choices.text: `shelves.length = 6;`
choices.why: `length` is final; the compiler refuses the assignment.

choices.text: Create a longer array, for example with `Arrays.copyOf(shelves, 6)`
choices.why: Right: a new array of six, with the old values copied and the new place at 0.

prompt: When is `for (int n : stock)` the better loop?
hint: What does it hand you, and what does it not?

choices.text: When you need to write a new value into each position
choices.why: It gives you the value and no position, so it cannot write into the array.

choices.text: When only the values matter
choices.why: Right: it cannot go out of bounds, as finding the largest value showed.

choices.text: When the array is longer than a thousand elements
choices.why: Both loops visit every element; length does not decide between them.

prompt: `Arrays.binarySearch(stock, 2)` on `{4, 0, 7, 2, 9}` printed `-1`, although 2 is at index 3. Why?
hint: What must be true of an array before a binary search?

choices.text: `binarySearch` only finds values at even positions
choices.why: There is no such rule; on the sorted copy it found 2 at index 1.

choices.text: Because `stock[0]` had been changed to 100 by then
choices.why: The search ran before the `alias` line changed anything.

choices.text: The array is not sorted, so the halving skips past it
choices.why: Right: on an unsorted array it answers wrongly and says nothing.

choices.text: `-1` means found at the last position, counting backwards
choices.why: A negative result means not found; it is not a position.

prompt: `int[] alias = stock; alias[0] = 100;` What does `stock[0]` hold afterwards?
hint: How many arrays exist after the first statement?

choices.why: Right: both variables refer to the same array, so the change shows through either.

choices.text: 4, its original value, because `alias` is a copy
choices.why: Assignment copies the reference, not the array; `Arrays.copyOf` makes copies.

choices.text: Nothing: two variables may not name the same array, so it fails to compile
choices.why: It compiles and runs; sharing one array between variables is ordinary.

prompt: `copy` was made with `Arrays.copyOf(stock, stock.length)`. Which of these print `true`? Choose all that apply.
hint: One operator asks about identity, one method about contents.

choices.text: `copy == stock`
choices.why: Two different arrays: `false`.

choices.text: `Arrays.equals(copy, stock)`
choices.why: Yes: same length and the same elements in order.

choices.text: `copy.length == stock.length`
choices.why: Yes: the copy was made at the same length.

choices.text: `copy.equals(stock)`
choices.why: An array's own `equals` is identity, the same as `==`: `false`. That is why `Arrays.equals` exists.

prompt: `Arrays.copyOf(stock, 7)` on a five-element `int` array returns a seven-element one. How many of its places hold 0 that were not copied from `stock`?
hint: The extra places get the default.

prompt: `int[][] grid = new int[3][4];` What are `grid.length` and `grid[0].length`?
hint: Rows first.

choices.text: 12 and 4
choices.why: `grid.length` is the outer array's length, the number of rows; there is no total of cells.

choices.text: 3 and 4
choices.why: Right: three rows, each of four.

choices.text: 4 and 3
choices.why: The first number in `new int[3][4]` is the number of rows.

prompt: `int[][] shelves = {{1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5, 6}};` Is this legal, and what is `shelves[1].length`?
hint: Each row is its own array.

choices.text: Illegal: every row of a two-dimensional array must have the same length
choices.why: Rows are separate arrays, so their lengths are independent; this is a jagged array.

choices.text: Legal, and 3, the length of the longest row
choices.why: Each row answers its own length.

choices.text: Legal, and 1
choices.why: Right: the second row holds only `4`.

choices.text: Legal, and 0, because the short rows are padded to the longest
choices.why: Nothing is padded; `{4}` is an array of length 1.

prompt: `int[][] jagged = new int[2][]; jagged[0] = new int[3];` Then `System.out.println(jagged[1].length);`. What happens, and why?
hint: What was `jagged[1]` set to?

choices.text: It prints 0, the length of an empty row
choices.why: No row was created there, not even an empty one.

choices.text: It prints 3, copying the length of the row before it
choices.why: Rows are independent; nothing copies lengths between them.

choices.text: It throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, because index 1 does not exist
choices.why: Index 1 exists in the outer array of two; it holds `null`.

choices.text: It throws `NullPointerException`: the row was never created
choices.why: Right: `jagged[1]` is `null`, and `null` has no length.

prompt: Run from source, the `NullPointerException` named `"<local4>[1]"`; after `javac -g` it named `"jagged[1]"`. What made the difference?
hint: What does the class file keep about local variables?

choices.text: `-g` makes the JVM check arrays more carefully
choices.why: The check and the exception were the same; only the wording of the name changed.

choices.text: `-g` keeps local variable names in the class file
choices.why: Right: without them the JVM can only number the variable, and `jagged` is local 4.

choices.text: The source launcher renames variables to save memory
choices.why: It compiles the same way plain `javac` does, without variable names; nothing is renamed.

prompt: Match each call to what it printed in `Grid.java`.
hint: Look at the transcript.

prompt: Which loop header visits every index of `int[] a` exactly once?
hint: Start at 0, stop before the length.

choices.text: `for (int i = 1; i <= a.length; i++)`
choices.why: It skips index 0 and then reads one past the end.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++)`
choices.why: The last pass reads `a[a.length]`, which throws.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)`
choices.why: Right: from 0 up to `length - 1`.

choices.text: `for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++)`
choices.why: It stops one short and never reads the last element.

prompt: Put the steps in order to find whether 7 is in `int[] stock` with `binarySearch`, without changing `stock`.
hint: Never sort the original.
items: Read a negative result as "not there"

prompt: A method receives `int[] scores`, sorts it with `Arrays.sort(scores)` to find the median, and returns. The caller then prints its own array. What does the caller see?
hint: How many arrays are there?

choices.text: Its array sorted, because the method sorted the same array
choices.why: Right: the parameter refers to the caller's array; copy it first to leave it alone.

choices.text: Its array in the original order, because the method had a copy
choices.why: Passing an array passes a reference to it, not a copy; lesson 30 is about exactly this.

choices.text: A compile error, because a method may not change its parameters
choices.why: Methods may change the objects their parameters refer to, and this one did.

prompt: Which call prints the elements of `int[] years` as `[1899, 1880, 1943]`?
hint: A helper in `java.util`.

choices.text: `System.out.println(years)`
choices.why: That prints `[I@` and a number.

choices.text: `System.out.println(years.toString())`
choices.why: The same thing: an array has no `toString` of its own that lists elements.

choices.text: `System.out.println(Arrays.toString(years))`
choices.why: Right.

prompt: `{{1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5, 6}}`: how many arrays exist in memory, counting the outer one?
hint: The figure in section 04.
